newsitem.title: ROMANIA: FEATURE - Romanians united as reforms start to bite.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Romanians united as reforms start to bite.

text.p: Romanians, hit by soaring inflation and falling incomes, seem determined to bite the bullet of faster reforms, believing it is vital to haul their country out of economic misery and put it on a firm growth path.

Reformers who took over government from former communists after a general election in November promised that a "work, sweat and austerity" package of measures would bring brighter days within a year or so.
"We have been living deprived lives for seven years, how much more could another one or two years hurt?," Florin Popescu, a pensioner in Bucharest told Reuters.
After growing more than 10 percent in 1995 and 1996, the economy is expected, at best, to stagnate or contract by up to two percent under the impact of tight monetary and fiscal policies.

"We are at an early stage of reform implementation. There are still blank spots and the uphill battle has started only now," said central bank chief economist Daniel Daianu. "But the thing to be noticed is that people seem aware that tough reforms are vital and so far they have shown patience."

Analysts of economic affairs say the fear of slipping into a chaos like that in neighbouring Bulgaria, where inflation is much higher and the economic crisis more severe, is what makes Romanians brace for radical reforms with patience.
"Clearer explanations from the government of what lies in store seems to help too," one analyst said.
PRICE LIBERALISATION ALREADY IN PLACE

The new government of Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea has started the shock therapy by freeing prices of basic goods, such as fuel, energy and food. This pushed month-on-month inflation to a 45-month peak of 18.8 percent in February. The year-on-year inflation reached 105.4 percent up from 76 a month earlier. The test was a rough one for Romanians, who make the equivalent of an average $80 a month.

The central bank has tightened money supply by soaking up liquidity through less financing for banks and freezing soft loans for farmers. Interest rates soared to an annual 150 percent on one-month deposits from some 50 percent in the New Year.

A removal of foreign exchange market curbs imposed by the previous government allowed the local leu currency, held artificially high in 1996, to slip towards what dealers say are realistic values. The currency plunged to 8,700 to the dollar on February 24 from about 4,000 at the start of the year, but later recovered slightly and is now hovering between 6,500 and 7,000.

A depreciated currency improved the current account flows, with the monthly deficit likely to have fallen to $100 million in February from $400 million in January. This year's target is to slash the deficit to $1.4 billion from an estimated $2.3 billion last year.
As part of the reform effort, the government approved on Saturday a tight 1997 budget, envisaging slashing the consolidated deficit to 4.5 percent of gross domestic product from 5.8 percent in 1996.

Earlier, the cabinet launched legislation allowing faster privatisation and the restructuring of communist-era industries. The reforms are due to pave the way for renewed credits from the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank.
RESTRUCTURING INEFFICIENT INDUSTRY IS TOP CHALLENGE
The reform moves are expected to trigger higher unemployment -- running now at 7.1 percent -- after state-run loss-making firms are shut down or liquidated.
"The thorniest issue will be imposing tough budgetary and financial discipline and closing down the most inefficient companies," Daianu said.
Economists say restructuring moves, though harsh, are essential to give support to a recent drive to tighten monetary policies if growth is to follow lower inflation and stable currency.
"A tougher monetary policy can yield results for a limited time unless it is backed by structural moves in the real economy," a local economist said.
The government aims to cut monthly inflation to some 2.2 percent in the last few months of 1997.
FAST LEGISLATIVE TRACK ESSENTIAL TO KEEP MOMENTUM

The government has set an ambitious end-April deadline to bring in or amend around 50 laws and decrees, including those on selling state banks, regulating bank insolvency, company restructuring, foreign investment, stock exchange and concessions.
Parliament, where the new ruling coalition has a comfortable majority, is expected to pass the 1997 budget bill in emergency procedures to earn international lenders' support.

Romania hopes to get around $1 billion in total loans from the IMF and World Bank to back up reforms. Both lenders withheld funds for Romania in 1996 because of the former ruling leftists' failure to live up to promised reforms.
The European Union also pledged to disburse 70 million Ecus ($80.2 million) in assistance for Romania this year, along with another $140 million from the G-24 group of industrialised countries.

Analysts expected what one called "a legislative big-bang" with the government ready to rule by decree, if parliament allows it, to push ahead with reforms and draw much-needed foreign direct and portfolio investment.
Last month, the Senate passed a bill giving foreigners the right to buy land in Romania. The bill has yet to clear the lower house.
FOREIGN INVESTMENT BADLY NEEDED TO REVAMP INDUSTRY
In stark contrast to his Socialist predecessors, most of whom paid lip service to foreign investment, Ciorbea has promised an investment heaven in Romania.
He told foreign investors they should not neglect the country, whose 22 million population makes it Eastern Europe's second-largest market after Poland.
Foreign investment in Romania has grown at a meagre $300 million to $400 million annually, and totals about a tenth of what neighbouring Hungary has attracted over the past seven years.
Ciorbea invited foreign companies to buy stakes in state utilities, communications and oil plants and vowed to cut red tape, often cited as a major obstacle by foreign investors.
The new openness stems from the conviction that the more advanced reformers in former Communist Europe are succeeding thanks to foreign investment which has revitalised their industries.
"Bear in mind that restructuring in more developed East European states has been based on foreign inflows. So the ball is now not only in our field," the central bank's Daianu said.

Analysts say Romania needs up to $2.5 billion annually to advance with market reforms, but they agree it needs to show solid performance to start attracting more money. ($ = 0.873 European Currency Unit ECUs)
